en: When the Buddha entered nirvana, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada was filled with sorrowful longing.
The translator’s name is lost; it is now appended to the Qin Records.
The World-Honored One, the Muni, lay with his head to the north amidst the śāla groves in the city of Kuśinagara.
When he first entered nirvana, Guhyapāda the Vajrapāṇi, seeing that the Buddha had passed into extinction, was filled with grief and distress, and spoke these words:
"The World-Honored One has accomplished the most supreme and unsurpassed ten powers; how is it that he is now defeated by such frailty, impermanence, and feeble vigor?"

The Tathāgata has abandoned me and entered into parinirvāṇa; from this day forth, I am without refuge, without support, without shelter, and without protection. Misery, affliction, and calamities have all at once gathered upon me, and the poisoned arrow of sorrow has deeply pierced my heart.

After Guhyapāda Vajrapāṇi had spoken these words, his longing for the World-Honored One caused the fire of grief to blaze even more fiercely; his inner organs were torn asunder and his heart and backbone were crushed. He fell to the ground, writhing and fainting like a collapsing cliff, remaining prostrate for a long time before he finally regained consciousness.
He immediately rose and sat up, weeping with sobs and stifled cries, and said with a choked voice:
"How strange! How strange!
The Mara of Death is most evil!"
"This mass of immeasurable merit and perfections has been destroyed by that Mara of Death.
He spoke further, saying:
"I only pray that the True Savior will arise for my sake; I am now of meager fortune and have no place of refuge."
"Why has the Blessed One abandoned me and entered parinirvāṇa alone?

From this day forward, I shall forever be deprived of his compassionate countenance. The Blessed One is now stilled; his bodily, verbal, and mental activities can no longer be beheld, nor can the Buddha Bhagavān be seen again entering the Buddha-abodes."

"When the Tathāgata formerly entered the Buddha-abiding samādhi, his majestic virtue and radiance were twice as brilliant and exquisite as usual; the Tathāgata’s face was fresh and lustrous, surpassing a newly blossomed lotus, like the rising sun illuminating the morning light—such a supreme countenance could no longer be seen."

When the Tathāgata is amidst the great assembly, he utters a great thunderous sound and a subtle, wondrous voice that cannot be heard by others; his words are truthful and non-dual, free from faults and afflictions, devoid of flattery or deceit, easy to understand, and beloved by all.
Within this world, there is nothing that surpasses the Buddha-dharma for eradicating all evils and reaching the City of Ambrosia (Amṛta). Alas!
The True Savior has entered eternal Nirvana, leaving all sentient beings without protection as they dwell within the vast wilderness of birth and death.
Furthermore, being without eyes and deprived of a guide, who shall show us the way?
"The Tathāgata’s dense clouds, capable of raining down ambrosia, have been extinguished by the wind of impermanence."
All sentient beings are scorched by the fire of craving; now that the Buddha has entered nirvana, who will rain down the rain of Dharma to extinguish that fire?
The Tathāgata has now ceased conditioned existence and attained the Unsurpassed Way to act as the Great Physician-King for all sentient beings.

All worlds are afflicted by the suffering of the disease of afflictions; now that you have entered nirvana, who will take pity on us and transform us with the True Path to heal the maladies of the fetters of all sentient beings?

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is known as one who knows gratitude and remembers kindness. Since the time I was in the womb, I have followed the Tathāgata like a shadow follows a form; I have harmonized with him and served him in obedience, never failing or neglecting my duty. Why, then, does he not respond to my utmost sincerity, but instead abandons me so utterly, as if I were someone who has betrayed his kindness?
"Alas, how strange! Oh, what great suffering!
For whom should this vajra be used for protection?
I shall cast it away immediately."
From this day forward, whom shall I serve?
Who will compassionately instruct and admonish me?
When shall I behold your venerable countenance again?
The World-Protecting Kings, in order to manifest the nectar of immortality, have sent me here to protect the Buddha; how is it that today you suddenly abandon us and enter into parinirvāṇa?
"My very life depends upon the Buddha; once he abandons me, upon whom shall I rely to sustain this life? Alas!
He who truly delivers all beings with compassion, who constantly proclaims the sublime Dharma to illuminate the darkness of ignorance—why does he now suddenly remain silent?"
“The Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) surpasses all that is above it; he has always been one who, being bound by a karmic affinity with sentient beings, desired to benefit them.
Where has he gone this very day?”
Yet today you have suddenly become silent and withdrawn, no longer rescuing those who seek transformation under your guidance.
When the various Māras and wicked people see the Buddha enter nirvana, they all rejoice greatly.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, acted as a great mariner upon the ocean of birth and death, yet today he has forever abandoned the work of ferrying beings across.

These sentient beings have followed the current of birth and death for immeasurable eons; only the Tathāgata is able, by means of the True Path, to cause all sentient beings to turn back that current.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has eternally severed all afflictions and serves as a great illumination for sentient beings shrouded in ignorance and darkness; yet today he enters parinirvāṇa, and the sentient beings of the world will see their darkness increase, forever obscured by nescience.
Vajrapāṇi, crying out in grief and distress, spoke these words again:
"World-Honored One, you are fully endowed with all the marks—the thirty-two marks of a Great Man born of a hundred merits—how can they be destroyed and forever beyond sight?"
"Alas, the destroyer of Māra!
Alas, the turner of the wheel of Dharma!
Alas, the one who extinguishes the firefly-like glimmers of all non-Buddhist heretics!"
Alas, the one who can destroy the body of existence!
Alas, the citadels of all wisdom!
Alas, the lamp of the Dharma, extinguished by the wind of impermanence!
"Alas! Dharmacandra has been swallowed and extinguished by the Rāhu of death!
He further spoke these words:
"O Great Tranquility, True Deliverance!"
I pray that you will tell me: where have you gone this very moment?
To what place have you arrived?
To which country have you departed?
Have you gone to Śrāvastī, Rājagṛha, Kapilavastu, or Vārāṇasī?
In which of these countries do you dwell?
And where, in what grove, are you staying now?
Is he in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, the Āmra Grove, or the Jeta Grove?
Among these groves, in which one is he?
And on which mountain is he?
Are you on Mount Svasukha, Mount Vindhya, or Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa?
Among all these mountains, which one do you occupy?
I pray that you tell me exactly where you truly are.
“The eight classes of beings—the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth—seeing that I always follow the Buddha, might ask me:
‘Where has the Buddha gone?’”
"How could I possibly find words with which to respond to him?

'In the past, when the World-Honored One was teaching sentient beings, even when he grew slightly weary and briefly lay down to rest, he focused his mind on clarity for the benefit of sentient beings.'"
"Why do you now abandon all beings and enter parinirvāṇa forever, no longer bringing them benefit?
True Savior! I pray that you will arise for my sake."
The fire of my grief and sorrow blazes within my breast, and my life is on the verge of being extinguished; I pray you grant me a single word, like cold water to quench this blazing fire.
I am now bitten by the venomous snake of sorrow and suffering; I pray you grant me the *agada* medicine of the Dharma to remove this poison.
The poisonous arrow of lamentation has pierced deep into my heart; I pray you grant me the tongs of your speech to extract it for me.
"All sentient beings suffer the pain of separation from those they love, yet the Tathāgata constantly preaches various dharmas for them to eliminate their afflictions.
Why alone do you not take pity on me and extinguish these manifold sufferings for my sake?"

"As I am now, overcome by grief and shrouded in darkness, unable to discern the truth and thus unable to release myself from the inner sickness of a grieving heart and its various delirious ravings—why does the World-Honored One not offer me consolation?"

My heart of reverence and obedience knows no weariness; I delight in beholding Your compassionate countenance without ever being satiated. Casting myself upon the ground, I pray only for a single glimpse of You—why does the World-Honored One not look upon me with compassion?
The Bull-King who has extinguished the fetters always carries me; why do you not lead me into Nirvana, leaving me alone and abandoned?
Having lost the Tathāgata, I am tormented by immeasurable and boundless sufferings, and I have not yet realized the Truths.
"Why have you alone been abandoned to enter nirvana?
How strange, how strange!
Will the Tathāgata sleep forever and never rise again?"
"Has the Tathāgata already departed and will not return?
He is like an extinguished lamp that never brightens again; like a collapsed jeweled tower that can never be rebuilt; like a submerged treasure trove that cannot be brought forth again."

Raising his hands, he cried out loudly, letting forth a voice of bitter weeping; like the rope supporting Śakra’s banner snapping, he fell to the ground and could not rise. Rolling about in lamentation, his heart, liver, throat, lips, and tongue were all parched. Dazed and bewildered, he collapsed to the earth and only regained consciousness after a long while.
Lovingly yearning for the Tathāgata’s body of merit, she grasped his feet marked with the *cakrāṅka* and embraced him tightly, refusing to let go, as she spoke these words:
“The Tathāgata’s feet are like the *utpala* flower and like the newly risen sun; they are pure and soft.”
The feet are firmly planted and possess soles marked with thousand-spoked wheels; such exquisite craftsmanship could not produce them through painting.
Although a Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses this mark, it is not clearly defined;
the Tathāgata’s wheel-mark is complete with spokes and hub, radiant and manifest.

His fingers were slender and long, closely joined and well-proportioned without being sparse; his nails were red and lustrous like polished copper; the webbing between his hands and feet was like that of a king of geese; and his body was full and fleshy, without visible veins or wrinkles in the skin.
The celestial kings, the human kings, the various kingly spirits, and the dragon kings all prostrated with their celestial crowns at the Buddha’s feet.
Having traversed the worlds with his wheel-marked feet in order to transform all those with whom he has a karmic connection, these feet now have no further use.

"In former days, my mind was always filled with joy; now that you have entered parinirvāṇa, you no longer cause me to experience such delight. This impermanence is an extreme evil, for it can destroy immeasurable merit and inconceivable forms."
“The majestic power of the Tathāgata can cause those who behold him to experience joy in body and mind; the immeasurable power of merit sustains the body of the Tathāgata.
Yet the power of impermanence is truly supreme, for it can bring the Tathāgata to the place of death.”

Even by means of the power of the milk nourished by his parents, the power of meditative concentration, the power of wisdom, and the power of supernormal faculties—by all these powers—the Tathāgata cannot extricate himself from the power of impermanence.
“Ānanda once entreated the World-Honored One to remain for the duration of a kalpa; why did the Tathāgata not accept his request?

Did the True Savior not, in the past, perform hundreds of thousands of ascetic practices throughout three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, being able to relinquish all things most difficult to give up? Did he not serve and attend upon various Buddhas for countless kalpas, making offerings and seeking omniscience in order to save sentient beings?”
In such a short time, those to be delivered have been few, and he has already entered nirvana.
When the Tathāgata was a bodhisattva in the past, he never grew weary while transforming sentient beings; how could he now be subject to exhaustion?
“Sentient beings amidst the turbid dharmas are like newborn calves filling twelve yojanas; how can you wean them from their milk and abandon them?
Please rise for my sake and provide these calves of the turbid dharma with a full measure of sweet milk.”
"At that time, Śakra and several billion devas came wishing to pose difficult questions; why do you not explain them for their sake?
Brahmā, the Lord of a thousand worlds, joins his palms and requests the Dharma; why do you not today preach the essentials of the Dharma to fulfill his aspirations?"

King Vaiśravaṇa is surrounded by tens of millions of yakṣas; Dhṛtarāṣṭra is surrounded by hosts of gandharvas; Virūḍhaka is surrounded by hosts of kumbhāṇḍas; Virūpākṣa is surrounded by hosts of nāgas—all such multitudes have come here for the sake of drinking the nectar of the Dharma. Why does the Tathāgata not use his excellent medicine to save those who are afflicted by disease?
The various assemblies of non-Buddhists revile the Dharma; why do you not swiftly arise to destroy their false doctrines?
The Lord of the Desire Realm causes disorder everywhere; why do you not subdue him?
"O Tathāgata!

These śrāvakas possess little wisdom, do not diligently practice recitation, and weary of extensive teachings; why do you not quickly arise and preach a concise summary for them, so that they may know the right path?"

Yet now Ānanda is the Buddha’s close attendant, serving the World-Honored One; since he has not yet severed the fetters at their very root, why does he not instruct him so that all fetters may be exhausted?
"Alas, how strange!
That such a person of firm substance and great merit has suddenly perished; this impermanence is like the elephant Dhanapāla, destroying countless beings."

This elephant Dhanapāla’s body is as vast as a mountain; since the Tathāgata was able to tame such a great elephant in the past, why is it that he is now, in turn, tamed by impermanence and brought even to total extinction?

Just as the Apara dragon can destroy Magadha by raising great clouds and thunder, with blazing flashes of lightning and raining down massive hailstones that break and snap trees, yet the Tathāgata was able to subdue that dragon of great power;
now, however, he has instead been overcome and carried away by impermanence.
Just as [the Buddha] was able to tame that fierce and cruel man Aṅgulimāla—that unruly person who could not be subdued—now the Muni, the World-Honored One, has been destroyed by impermanence.
Just as a malevolent spirit in the wilderness might slaughter all beings until the land is left empty, yet one can still tame it and cause it to uphold the precepts;
now, however, it has entered the snare of impermanence and is utterly destroyed without remainder.

Just as when Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa was stained by attachment to me and submerged within the thicket of false views—so difficult to extract—the Tathāgata still felt compassion for him and manifested eighteen kinds of miraculous transformations to bring him to subjection;
yet now he has been toppled by impermanence.
"All sentient beings are impoverished of merit; the great ocean of wisdom has been dried up by the sun of impermanence;
Mount Sumeru of right knowledge has been shattered by the vajra-thunderbolt of impermanence;
and the Bodhi-tree of the Buddha’s virtues—abounding with the exquisite flowers of the awakening-mind and the fruits of the Path—has been cut down and destroyed by the axe of impermanence."
The vast light of wisdom—whose fame resounds throughout the world and which can burn away the fuel of all that is born—is extinguished by the waters of impermanence.

Excessive power is impermanent and lacks any guiding dharma; it cannot be restrained by the wise, nor can it be avoided by those who possess diligence, watchfulness, courage, fierce vigor, renown, a gentle mind, or the tranquility of disciplined faculties.
"Alas, impermanence!
How cruel and violent it is, making no distinction between good and evil; it can destroy both the virtuous and the non-virtuous alike.

As he spoke these words, the earth shook violently, mountain peaks collapsed, great stars fell, fires broke out in the four directions, the sun, moon, and all the constellations lost their radiance, and all devas and humans were devoid of joy.

“Now my body is so weak that I cannot even lift it; I feel as though I am sinking into the earth. My vision blurs with yellow and black, my mind is disordered, and I have forgotten what I was thinking. My lips are parched and my tongue is dry; my speech is faltering and my voice is broken and raspy. Death is near, and my life will surely end this very moment. The Buddha has departed, leaving me behind.”
Thus, this great multitude uttered various cries of lamentation and spoke hundreds of thousands of words, longing for the Buddha.
Śakra addressed them, saying:
"Cease, cease! It is enough!"
"Do you not now recall the few words of the Great Sage?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they have no abiding nature, they cannot be relied upon, and they are subject to change.'"
All that is gathered must disperse; all that meets must part; all that is born must die.

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like trees standing on a steep riverbank, like drawings on water that vanish as soon as they are drawn, like bubbles or dew on a blade of grass that cannot remain for long, and like a city of the Gandharvas that appears momentarily before the eye.

Human life is as swift as a drawn arrow; its rapid passage through the world is swifter than the sun and moon. Human life passes even more quickly than these celestial bodies; one should understand that it is impermanent and subject to decay.
If there is anything remaining incomplete in the Buddha’s work, he will not enter *nirvāṇa*; only when the Buddha’s work is fully accomplished will he enter *nirvāṇa*.

He entrusts this Buddha-dharma to humans and devas, and with this grave responsibility, he gives it to his disciples, the *śrāvakas*, so that they may proceed toward the fearless state of quiescence, where all suffering is exhausted and rebirth is no longer received.
"You all should not give rise to great sorrow and distress.
Thus ends the *Buddha-entrance-into-nirvāṇa-mijue-jingang-lishi-ailian-jing* (The Sutra on the Buddha’s Entry into Nirvana and the Lamentation of the Secret-Trace Vajra-wielding Malla).
